glosses: The mode is the number that occurs most often in a group of numbers.

examples.text: In a normal distribution, with large sets, the mean, median and mode will typically be the same value.

glosses: A mode is specific a kind of clause that shows how the speaker feels about it. Modes show whether something is true, probably true, a wish, etc. Usually called mood.

examples.text: In Finnish, for example, the conditional mode is used both in the main clause and the subordinate.

glosses: The mode of a rock is the different minerals in it.
A mode is a specific pattern of wave movement.

examples.text: Under normal circumstances, there is no coupling between the two modes, which have different propagation constants.

glosses: Differentiation finding or showing the differences between things.

examples.text: In the shop, there was no differentiation between product from Asia and product from Europe.

glosses: Differentiation is the process of becoming or making something different.

examples.text: As the cells grow and divide, differentiation takes place. You can begin to see some as muscle cells, some as blood cells, etc.

glosses: Differentiation is acting different towards different people or situations.

examples.text: Schools tend to have little formal curricular differentiation between the sexes, except in physical education.

glosses: Differentiation is the process of obtaining the derivative of a function.
If you eliminate something, you make it go away or disappear, or you kill it.

examples.text: The recent fixes have eliminated the problems we were having.
Canada was eliminated in the first round of the world cup.
He was at risk of being eliminated by the other gang members.

glosses: A priority is something that is important; you want to do it first or spend more time or money on it than other things.

examples.text: Learning the language is a high priority for all people who move to the country.
The nineteen national priority areas will receive 70 per cent of the funding.

glosses: If something has or is given priority, it should go before other things.

examples.text: The Government needs to give a higher priority to the quality of life.
Teachers need to give priority to science over less important subjects.

glosses: An ideology is the set of beliefs behind a movement, religion, political group, etc.

examples.text: Schools reflect clearly the dominant political ideologies of their countries.
For many years the ideology of the Catholic church had a crushing effect on science.

glosses: The foundation of something is the basic ideas or work behind it.

examples.text: These early inventions laid the foundations of modern radio technology.
Her education gave her a solid foundation in all the major subjects.

glosses: The foundation of a building is the solid base that is under it and that supports it.

examples.text: They dug solid foundations, spending a lot of time pouring concrete into four pits.

glosses: A foundation is an organisation that collects money to do good things.

examples.text: The Open Software Foundation has opened up laboratories to test software.

glosses: The foundation of a group, business, country, etc. is the act of starting it.

examples.text: The company has double in size every year since its foundation.

glosses: Foundation is the first layer of cream or makeup.

examples.text: Dot the foundation over the face-on the nose, the cheeks, the chin and spread working from the face outwards.

glosses: The state or condition of being depraved; moral debasement.

examples.text: He was a very bad man, lost in depravity.

glosses: A very bad act or trait.

examples.text: Susan's depravity was her husband's murder.

glosses: Evil that is part of human nature, contamination by sin.

examples.text: Our depravity is the result of Adam's fall.

glosses: If something is ductile, it can be stretched into wire, usually metal.
If something is ductile, it can easily be molded into a new shape.
If someone is ductile, they are easily lead; they are prone to follow.
An adaptation is a change to fit a different situation or the result of that change, especially when a story goes from book to TV or movie.

examples.text: The new film adaptation of the classic book Little Women is quite wonderful.
He is also disabled and requires special adaptations to his home.

glosses: Adaptation is the process of changing to fit a different situation.

examples.text: These products undergo a constant process of change and adaptation.

glosses: Something is called edible if it can be eaten by humans and animals without danger to their health.

examples.text: These mushrooms are edible.

glosses: An edible is something that you can eat.

examples.text: The apple is an edible.

glosses: A quotation is a sentence or phrase that was said by someone and is now being used or referred to by somebody else. Quotations can be from books, movies, speeches, television shows, songs, etc.

examples.text: This chapter began with a quotation from Monica Furlong.
Consider the following quotation from the Bible: Job 16:18: "O earth, cover not thou my blood."

glosses: Quotation is the act of using somebody else's exact words.
A quotation is a report of the cost or value of something.
To use someone's exact words.

examples.text: Did he quote me in the newspaper?

glosses: A quote is somebody's exact words used by somebody else.

examples.text: In the following quote, a young woman describes her experience with drugs.
I might also include a quote from Shakespeare: "All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players".

glosses: A quote is a report of the cost or value of something.
If something is absent, it means to be not in a place or missing.

examples.text: John is absent from school today.

glosses: When you absent yourself from something, you do not turn up for it and not appear.

examples.text: John absented himself from the meeting as he had something on.

glosses: Absent means without or barring.

examples.text: Absent any problems, we should be finished in two hours.

glosses: An effective strategy, treatment, method, etc is one that works well as planned.

examples.text: Teachers are using instructional strategies that are most effective in helping students learn.

glosses: If you have effective command, consent, control, etc., you have it in practice but not officially.

examples.text: The students had effective control over what the teacher would include on the test.

glosses: If a law, agreement, change, etc. becomes effective, it officially begins.

examples.text: The new rules about ball size are effective next season.

glosses: You use effective to tell when something starts officially.

examples.text: Effective next week, all employees will wear the new uniform.

glosses: If something is preliminary, it is a preparation for a main matter.
A preliminary is a preparation for a main matter.
before

examples.text: Preliminary to the main discussions, perhaps we could introduce ourselves.

glosses: If x happens regardless of y, y does not change x.

examples.text: She left, regardless of him asking her to stay.

glosses: If an act or idea is contrary to something, it is against it.

examples.text: The president's actions are contrary to the constitution and therefore illegal.

glosses: You use contrary to x when x is different from the truth.

examples.text: Contrary to popular belief, the oil companies cannot control the price of crude.
What she told me was contrary to everything I had ever heard.
Contrary to popular myth, women are not worse drivers than men.

glosses: A contrary view, sentence, etc. is opposite to other ones.

examples.text: The contrary view is that these kind of projects are a waste of money.
The only thoughts he had were contrary ones.

glosses: A contrary person tries to be different from other people or does not often agree with others.
The contrary is the opposite of an idea, sentence, etc.

examples.text: It is best to believe people are good, at least until the contrary is shown.
This is not necessarily bad; on the contrary, it is sometimes quite useful.

glosses: Successive things follow in order, one after another.

examples.text: Successive governments have refused to make the changes.
Edward Kawak won in four successive years (1982–1985).
Cancers were developing at younger and younger ages with each successive generation in each family.

glosses: Innovation is the process of making something new and original.

examples.text: Our company has stayed in the lead largely by encouraging innovation.

glosses: An innovation is something new and original.

examples.text: The number of technical innovations is growing at a faster and faster rate.

glosses: If you prohibit something, you say that it must not be done.

examples.text: The laws were changed to prohibit the use of certain tools.
Company policy is to prohibit dogs from entering the store.

glosses: If x prohibits y, y is not possible because of x.

examples.text: The use of a password prohibits access to outsiders.

glosses: If you isolate something, you make it so that it does not or cannot contact certain other things.

examples.text: We want to isolate ourselves from everyday worries.
The prisoner was isolated to protect him from attack.
Britain is isolated from the rest of Europe by the Channel.

glosses: An isolate is something that does not or cannot contact certain other things.

examples.text: A total of 296 isolates were recovered from 105 patients, 79 (75%) of whom were infected with mycobacteria.

glosses: An isolate is a language that has no known relatives.
If you isolate something, you make it so that it does not or cannot contact certain other things.

examples.text: We went to isolate ourselves from everyday worries.
The prisoner was isolated to protect him from attack.
Britain is isolated from the rest of Europe by the Channel.

glosses: If something is isolated it is alone.

examples.text: As she got older and her friends moved away, she became more and more isolated.

glosses: A problem is something that is difficult to do, understand, or believe.

examples.text: If you have a problems with the computer, I can probably help.
You should see your doctor if you think you have a health problem.
This book tells you how to deal with drinking problems.
If you are regularly late, it can cause problems.
Today, we are concerned with some serious problems with the product.
I solved the problem by replacing a broken part.
It's a good idea to discuss your problems with a friend.
Problems like these arise from a lack of care.
We've identified a number of problem areas that need to be looked at.

glosses: A problem is a question on a test.

examples.text: Most students got the right answer for the first problem.

glosses: You say "no problem" to agree to do something.

examples.text: "Could you open the door for me?" "Sure, no problem!"

glosses: You say "no problem" after somebody thanks you or apologises to you.

examples.text: "Thank you so much for all your help." "No problem! Any time!"

glosses: If you eat something, usually food, you put it in your mouth, chew it, and swallow it.

examples.text: I always eat too much good when it's Thanksgiving.
My 2 year old accidentally ate chalk that she found on the table.

glosses: If you eat the cost of something, you pay for it.

examples.text: The supplier will have to eat the cost of returning the goods.

glosses: If you eat someone, you give them sex with your mouth (oral sex)
Humor that is not serious but is meant to mimic. Saying something you don't mean, to be funny or to make someone feel bad.

examples.text: "No, I don't want any food, I'm just standing here holding an empty plate to make my fingers stronger," he said with sarcasm.

glosses: If you think that something is or may be true, you feel that it is or may be true.

examples.text: You know you can't do that. What were you thinking?
Some people think this is a good idea, but I don't think so.
I think the best thing to do now is to go home.
I just thought you might want some coffee.
I really think you should stop seeing her.
What do you think about the new teacher?
Vancouver is thought to be a good place to live.
I think he's a doctor.
I think she wants us to go that way.
I thought I saw something.
"Is this right?" "I think so."

glosses: If you think about something, you use your mind to give it your attention.

examples.text: "What's the best way?" "I'm not sure. Let me think."
All day I was thinking about my sister in Lisbon.
I don't want to think about that right now.
Just think how nice it will be when we're finished.

glosses: You use think when you have words or ideas in your mind without saying them out loud.

examples.text: "It's no good," she thought.

glosses: You use think in suggestions and requests.

examples.text: I was thinking we could go out tonight.
Do you think you could help me here?

glosses: If you don't think to do something, you don't remember to do it.

examples.text: I didn't think to ask her.
I can't think where my keys are.

glosses: If you say you'll have a think about something, it means you'll give it your attention.
If you highlight something, you make it more noticeable or obvious.

examples.text: I usually use a pen to highlight the important section in my textbook.
Let me just highlight this point since many people misunderstand it.

glosses: If you highlight your hair, you make some parts a lighter colour.
A highlight is a particularly good part.

examples.text: The chicken was the highlight of the dinner, just amazing.
I didn't see the game, but I watched the highlights on the news.

glosses: A highlight is a light-coloured area.

examples.text: The shirt was blue with yellow highlights.

glosses: An inspection is a careful look at something, usually for problems.

examples.text: Before the flight, the pilot did a complete inspection of the airplane.
It seemed that he had not been paid, but upon closer inspection it was found that he had indeed.
An inspection of the prison was planned for next week.

glosses: Termination is the act of ending something.

examples.text: We will continue to do business in Asia after termination of the Japan program.

glosses: The termination is the end point, time or limit of something.

examples.text: Three years after the termination of war in 1945, France was fighting another war in Indo-China.

glosses: Termination is when you lose your job.

examples.text: The company will cut costs through the termination of 150 employees.

glosses: Termination is the act of killing something.

examples.text: The group is against the termination of these sick babies.

glosses: A termination is a suffix or the end of a word.

examples.text: The termination of a verb in the past tense is usually "ed".

glosses: Displacement is when something is made to move out of its place.

examples.text: The war has caused the displacement of tens of thousands of people.
The displacement of folk music by western pop music has happened in many countries.

glosses: Displacement is the amount of liquid or gas that is moved when something floats in it.
Restraint is the quality people show when they don't do something they shouldn't do.

examples.text: You already ate too much cake. Now please show some restraint.

glosses: A restraint is a strap or other thing that holds a person in place, like a seatbelt in a car or handcuffs that the police use to hold someone.

examples.text: A baby needs the right kind of restraint to ride safely in a car.

glosses: A restraint is something that stops people from doing something.

examples.text: A legal restraint prevents him from going to meet his ex-girlfriend.

glosses: If you reinforce something, you make it stronger.

examples.text: Recent mistakes only reinforce the view that nobody cares.
Hitting a child can reinforce his tendency to use violence.
This meeting has helped to further reinforce the links between the colleges.
The steel is used to reinforce the building's walls.
The extra men will reinforce the army in Iraq.

glosses: If x denotes y, x is a sign of or has the meaning of y.

examples.text: The term "sales mix" is used to denote the percentage of total sales of each product.
In this text, ungrammatical sentences are denoted by an asterisk (*).

glosses: If x offsets y, the loss (because) of y is balanced by x.

examples.text: The school will provide limited scholarships to offset the cost of tuition.

glosses: If you offset x against y, you compare of contrast them.

examples.text: All this solid colour is offset by the tiny yellow green flowers.

glosses: The past tense and past participle of offset.
An offset is something that balances (the loss of) something else.

The image produced by this kind of printing.

The act of obeying orders from others.

examples.text: Obedience is very important in any army.

glosses: behavior in which you do what good person, father, boss, teacher, tells you to do.

examples.text: He showed cowardice when he ran away and left his friend to fight the other children.

glosses: Exploitation is the use of something, usually for profit.

examples.text: The commercial exploitation of Alaska for oil could lead to serious environmental problems.

glosses: Exploitation is the use or treatment of someone unfairly.

examples.text: Today, most countries have laws against the exploitation of children in factories.

glosses: If you detect something, you use your senses to find or notice it.

examples.text: Some insects can detect changes in temperature as small as 0.003 degrees Celsius.
These animals have a smell that even a human nose can easily detect.
The chemical has been detected in lakes and rivers, in fish and birds, and in human breast milk.
Our instruments are not sensitive enough to detect it.

glosses: If you abandon something, you go away from it with no plan to return.

examples.text: Many teens abandon all chances of a successful future when they drop out of school.
After much thought, they abandoned the idea as being too difficult.
The government abandons after-school programs when money is tight.

glosses: If you abandon something, you give up control of it.

examples.text: They danced wildly down the street, abandoning themselves to the night and the moon.
The woodcutter and his wife considered abandoning Hansel and Gretel in the forest.

glosses: Abandon is a state where you do not control yourself.

examples.text: In these games, kids shoot and blow each other up with reckless abandon.
The man dove into the pool with reckless abandon.

glosses: RAM is the acronym for random access memory.
If something is random, there is no purpose, reason, or pattern.

examples.text: I have to sit there like typing in random keywords to see if it's a keyword.
Why don't you get organised instead of just contacting random people.

glosses: If a process is random, every option has an equal chance of happening.

examples.text: 20 per cent of the random sample of the libraries were public in any normal sense of the word.
Banks use random numbers to make codes to keep your computer banking safe and secret.

glosses: A revision is a change or edit a to language, a plan, etc.

examples.text: This book needs a lot of revision before it can be published.
She revised what she said so that she was not saying something bad about him.
The plan has undergone a number of complete revisions.

glosses: A revision is a piece of writing or plan that has changed or will change.

examples.text: The software includes the latest revisions to the HTML standards.

glosses: In the UK, revision is the process of studying something again.

examples.text: I need to do more revision for the test.

glosses: Just about; almost but not quite

examples.text: Once you put it on, it is virtually impossible to remove.
Car theft became so common that private cars virtually disappeared from the area.

glosses: If someone devotes time or energy to something, they feel that it is important and they spend a lot of time or energy on it.

examples.text: I devoted ten years of my life to writing that book.
She decided to devote her life to nursing.

glosses: When someone refines something, they make it better.

examples.text: We need to refine our way of organizing this office.

glosses: When people refine a food or other thing, they make it purer.

examples.text: They take sugar cane and refine it to make white sugar.

glosses: A very good understanding of something; a clear idea about how something works.

examples.text: We need to get some insight into the causes of this problem.
I just had a flash of insight about why she does that.

glosses: A violation of a rule is an act of breaking the rule: going past the limits of the rule.

examples.text: The speed you were driving your car was a violation of the speed limit.
Walking into my house like that was a violation of my privacy.
The new finding seems to be in violation of our understanding of physics.
This violation of our trust cannot be forgiven.
The violation of these young girls by a man their uncle is hard to understand.

glosses: Two things coincide with each other if they're both in the same place or at the same time.

examples.text: The time of your party coincides with my niece's wedding, so I can't come.
The end of one side of a triangle coincides with the end of another side, making a corner.

glosses: A medium amount is an amount that is not small and not large, but in the middle.

examples.text: Would you like a small, medium or large drink?

glosses: A medium is stuff that something moves through.

examples.text: Light can go through different media: air, water, glass.
Sound waves slow down when they go through this kind of medium.

glosses: A medium is a person who hears ideas that come from people who are dead. (plural mediums)

examples.text: We all closed our eyes, and the medium said "I hear your father speaking."
I don't believe those mediums can really hear anything.

glosses: A portion is a part of something.

examples.text: We need to put more signs up in this portion of the city.

glosses: A portion is an amount of food for one person.

examples.text: Each portion has six meatballs.

glosses: If you portion something out, you give parts of it to different people.

examples.text: They portioned out the water among them.

glosses: A reason, idea or writing is qualitative if it is about the way something is, or about the thing's qualities, but not about amounts.

examples.text: I have a qualitative idea of what his work is like, but I don't know how much work he's done.
Qualitative differences between advertisements are likely to be far more important than quite large differences in the number of advertisements.

glosses: A trigger is the part of a gun that you push with one finger when you want to make the gun shoot.

examples.text: I didn't want to make him angry, because he had his finger on the trigger.

glosses: A trigger is a little thing that makes something bigger happen.

examples.text: Bad smells are one of the triggers for my headaches.

glosses: A little thing triggers a big thing to happen when it causes it.

examples.text: Those angry words triggered the beginning of the war.

glosses: The format of some writing is the way it is organized: the size and colour of the letters, the way it is divided into parts, the kind of words used.

examples.text: What format do you want the report written in?

glosses: The format of some writing is the kind of computer program you need to be able to read it.

examples.text: I can't read that page you sent me. My computer doesn't read that format.

glosses: Something's format is its style, type, organisation, etc.

examples.text: The format of the meeting will be quite casual.

glosses: Someone formats some writing when make it have a particular format.

examples.text: How should I format the report?

glosses: Someone formats a computer disk when they prepare a disk for writing and reading.

examples.text: You need to format the disk before you can copy those files onto it.

glosses: Mediation is the process of helping two people or groups who are not in agreement to come to an agreement.

examples.text: When I was separated from my wife, we had mediation to help decide who got to keep the house.

glosses: Someone is mature if they act like an adult.

examples.text: You're not mature enough to do this job.

glosses: A living thing is mature if it has stopped growing physically.

examples.text: A mature female is about 30 kg.

glosses: Some kinds of food, such as wine, cheese, or fruit are mature when they are ready to eat or drink.
A mature person is older.

examples.text: Colleges are accepting more mature students and fewer kids out of high school.

glosses: If something is mature, it is fully developed.

examples.text: Television is a mature technology.

glosses: If movies, books, etc. are mature, they are meant for adults because they contain violence, sex, etc.
If something matures, it becomes fully developed.

examples.text: Along the way she has also matured into a beautiful young woman.
These problems have been solved as the technology has matured.

glosses: When something diminishes it gets smaller or less important or makes something that way.

examples.text: The way you talked just now diminished my respect for you.
The amount of water in the lake is diminishing because there has been no rain.

glosses: When x is analogous to y, it is similar to y.

examples.text: Using that little broom to sweep this big floor is analogous to using a candle to cook dinner for 40 people.
The development of the new DVD with multiple formats is analogous to the video wars between beta and VHS.

glosses: Something is temporary if it's only for a short time.

examples.text: A tent was our temporary home after our house burned down in the fire.
The middle of the floor is a temporary place for these books until I find room for them on the shelf.

glosses: A fluctuation is when something changes back and forth quickly.

examples.text: The price of wheat stayed the same, but there were a lot of fluctuations in the price of rice.
Every time a cloud goes past, there is a fluctuation in the amount of sunshine.

glosses: When something is minimal, it is very small or small enough to not be important, especially the smallest.

examples.text: We had a minimal amount of rain yesterday, so we still need to water the plants.
Don't worry -- any problems from this will be minimal.

glosses: Wages is the money a person is paid for doing their job.

examples.text: Only 6 percent of the wage earners in this country earn more than $ 100,000.
They are working for minimum wage or $5 an hour.
The workers were demanding higher wages.
The average hourly wage rose only 2.8% last year.

glosses: If you wage a battle, war, or campaign for or against something, you fight or work hard for or against it.

examples.text: After his death in 1990, a five-year battle was waged in court for control of the $72 million estate.
The Iranians hate Iraq for the war that they waged against them for eight years.
This is the beginning of a long legal battle, similar to the campaign waged against the tobacco industry.

glosses: Two things are incompatible with each other if they don't fit together or don't work well together.

examples.text: The husband and wife were not happy together because they were incompatible.
I can't fit this wire into my computer because the end is incompatible with the part of the computer for plugging things in.

glosses: ordinal eightieth) Eighty is the number 80.

examples.text: There were about eighty people at the party.

glosses: The number 80.

examples.text: Seventy plus ten is eighty.

glosses: If something commences, it begins.

examples.text: The school year commenced on Sept. 4.

glosses: Vision is being able to see with your eyes.

examples.text: Now I'm old and my vision is not very good, so I don't drive a car any more.

glosses: Vision is being able to think of good ideas for the future.

examples.text: This woman will be a good leader of our company because she has great vision about the future of our company.
The president needs to create ideas, to create a vision for the country.

glosses: Endemic means that a species (or other taxon) belongs to something else. If an animal is endemic to a place (or habitat), it only exists in that habitat.

examples.text: Some trout are endemic to Lake Baikal.

glosses: in an important or large enough way

examples.text: The price of gas dropped significantly today, causing drivers to line up at the pumps to fill up.
His face looked significantly different.
He was, significantly, at the shop just before the accident.

glosses: with a particular meaning

examples.text: He looked at her significantly.

glosses: My favorite brand is the brand I like most.

examples.text: Ford is my favorite brand of truck.

glosses: A favorite is a thing or person that someone likes the most. It is a thing that someone prefers, or likes more than any other.

examples.text: Chocolate ice cream is my favorite.

glosses: When kings and other royalty have favorites, these are people they trust.

examples.text: He was a favorite of the king.

glosses: Foreign means something that comes from a different place or country. Foreign people are known as foreigners.

examples.text: Sven has a foreign accent.

glosses: Foreign can mean something that is not familiar or not characteristic.

examples.text: Greed was as foreign to him as a Frenchman in China.

glosses: Something that is lying down or "straight across" is horizontal. In a horizontal direction means straight across.

examples.text: The road across the Nullabor plain is horizontal.
Dad hung a swing from a horizontal branch.
Horizontal stripes on a shirt make a person look wider.

glosses: To be horizontal means to have something to do with the horizon.
In a vertical direction or position.

examples.text: The cliffs fell vertically down to the sea.
The rocket shot vertically into the sky.

glosses: In a horizontal direction or position.

examples.text: The pictures were arranged horizontally around the room.
Johnnie's hat sailed horizontally out the window.

glosses: If you write a book, an article, a computer program, a piece of music, etc., you create it.

examples.text: My dream is to write a children's book.
Mozart wrote over 600 pieces of music during his lifetime.
He can't write. He's a terrible writer.
In the article, the author writes that these things need to change.

glosses: If you write, you use letters, numbers, or other marks on paper or on a computer to show words.

examples.text: Can you write your name and phone number here for me?
Our teacher taught us to write beautifully.
It's amazing how many people can't read and write.
Do you have any paper to write on?
Listen to what I say and write it down.

glosses: If you write, you send a letter to someone.

examples.text: Please, phone or write me when you have some time.
She would write to Mom every week and give her all the details.

glosses: (computer) If a computer writes, it records something in its memory or on a disk.

examples.text: Old computers were much slower at writing files.

glosses: in that way or by that means

examples.text: He pulled it closer to him, thereby making it far easier to get up.
Food product quality is more easily maintained thereby reducing spoilage losses.
Water reflects less light than ice, thereby allowing the oceans to absorb more heat from the sun.
I'm concerned by attempts to limit this right and thereby to limit our freedom.
Having missed the first bit, he listened closely to catch the rest, hoping thereby to reply sensibly.
This change would prevent the team (and thereby the school) from advancing.

glosses: A uniform is clothing that is very similar and worn by a group of people.

examples.text: All the young army men wore identical uniforms and badges of rank.
School uniform was always worn, which for the boys meant khaki shirts and trousers.
When I was a child, I was afraid of men in uniform: policemen, firemen, even the milkman.

glosses: If something is uniform, there is no variation in it.

examples.text: It was designed to be uniform from one end to the other.
The increase in grades has been uniform across all subjects except math.

glosses: mostly, mainly

examples.text: The predominantly male, white judges treat men and women differently.
Her work during this period was predominantly concerned with children learning to read.

glosses: A meaning that is implicit is understood or given but not directly.

examples.text: There is an implicit assumption that women should be acting more like men.
Though teachers may not formulate aims consciously, they will be implicit in the teaching.

glosses: A belief that is implicit is complete and without question.

examples.text: Jonadab was used to implicit obedience from his children and was surprised at his son's answer.

glosses: Clarity is the quality of being clear.

examples.text: She dreamed, with great clarity, that she had seen her own death.
Lack of clarity on the part of the teacher will cause confusion among the students.

glosses: Conformity is the state of being or becoming similar to other members of a group.

examples.text: In high school, students who do not show a high degree of conformity are often not accepted by other students.
Often the teaching of writing is really the teaching of social conformity: students must write like everyone else.

glosses: Conformity is the state of following rules or expectations.

examples.text: The army is there to ensure conformity with the UN resolutions.

glosses: A giant is a very big man or woman, often in fairy tales.

examples.text: Jack climbed the beanstalk and found a land ruled by a giant.

glosses: If a thing is giant, it is very big.

examples.text: He bought a giant doll at the fair.

glosses: If something is contemporary it is related to this time (now). Technically, this is an incorrect usage; better is to use "modern", "now" or "present-day".

examples.text: The artist has a great knowledge of the sources of historical and contemporary art.

glosses: If x is contemporary with y, they happened at about the same time.

examples.text: They are sources that are contemporary or near contemporary with the period being studied.

glosses: Somebody's contemporary is a person who lived at or near the same time.

examples.text: This is what made Marx so different from his socialist contemporaries.

glosses: If you breach a duty, you do something that you should not do.
If an army or the police breach a barrier, a wall, etc., they were not able to enter it before but now they can.

examples.text: The police breached the front door and searched the house.

glosses: A breach is the act of breaching; for example, a breach of contract may occur when somebody does not do what they promised.
A breach can also be a hole.

examples.text: Water entered through a breach in the levee.

glosses: To enter is to go into something.

examples.text: I entered the building through the side door.

glosses: To enter is to go in.

examples.text: Please pay the fare before you enter.

glosses: To type something into a computer.

examples.text: I entered all the necessary information but it still won't work.

glosses: "Enter" is a key on a computer keyboard.
A fare is money that you pay for public transportation; that is, to ride on a bus, taxi, train or airplane.

examples.text: The city is planning to increase its bus fares again.

glosses: A duty is something that you should do.

examples.text: Parents have the duty to educate their children.

glosses: A tax placed on imports or exports; a tariff, customs duty, excise duty.

examples.text: Import duty and taxes are due when importing goods into the United States.

glosses: To violate means to break something like a law.

examples.text: A person violated the copyright of a book.

glosses: If you neglect someone, you do not take care of them.
Neglect is the failure of somebody to do a duty.
A batter is somebody who is supposed to hit a ball with a bat.
A batter is a mixture of flour and liquid (usually eggs and water).
If you batter someone or something, you hit or beat it.

examples.text: The battered child was brought to the attention of the police.

glosses: If you beat someone or something, you hit it, usually many times.

examples.text: It made a loud noise when he beat the drum.
I had to leave and divorce my husband, because he kept beating and choking me.

glosses: If you beat a person or a team, you win and they lose.

examples.text: The best team usually beats the worst one.

glosses: The past tense of beat.
Beat is the rhythm of music.
A heartbeat.
If something happens automatically, it happens without the need for a person to start it or do anything more.

examples.text: The door closed and locked automatically behind him.
If you sign up for this, you'll automatically be entered in a contest to win a car.

glosses: If you do something automatically, you do it without thinking about it.

examples.text: If a man and woman spend time together, you shouldn't automatically assume they're lovers.
"You're welcome," she said automatically.

glosses: A handshake is when two people hold hands for a few seconds and move them up and down before letting go. It is often used like a greeting (like saying "hello" or "goodbye" when people meet) or to say that two people have agreed on something.

examples.text: When I meet someone, I give a firm handshake.

glosses: An heir is the person who gets the property or money when someone dies.

examples.text: Jack was his only heir, so he will get all the money.

glosses: The present participle of increase.

examples.text: His money is increasing because he makes good business deals.
He is worried about his increasing debt: it keeps getting bigger and bigger.

glosses: A grandchild is the grandson or granddaughter of someone. It is the child of someone's child.

examples.text: Jemima is my grandmother. She is my father's mother. I am her grandchild.

glosses: An incumbent is a person who currently holds a type of position, often in politics.

examples.text: She was an incumbent in the last election for the office she holds.

glosses: If someone is incumbent, they are in a political position now.

examples.text: They are incumbent in this election because they are in office.

glosses: When lines intersect, it means they meet at one point.

examples.text: Main Street intersects 10th Avenue here.

glosses: The place where two lines or segments meet is called an intersect.

examples.text: The intersect of line A and line B is at point X.

glosses: The wife of a person's son. The opposite of a daughter-in-law would be a son-in-law, or a daughter's husband.
You use plus when you add numbers.

examples.text: Two plus two is four. (2+2=4)
The TV is $299 plus tax.
The margin of error is plus or minus one per cent.

glosses: and also

examples.text: The farm has over 5,000 horses, plus a few cats and dogs.

glosses: You use plus after a number to mean more than or over.

examples.text: The country has a population of 3 million plus.
He got a B+ on his test.

glosses: A plus is a good thing.

examples.text: I know you don't like it, but there are big pluses about living here.
On the plus side though, it is small and easy to use.

glosses: A plus is a plus sign: +

examples.text: You don't have to write the plus in front of positive numbers, but always write the minus in front of negative numbers.

glosses: used before the last item in a list

examples.text: I like singing, reading, and tennis plus playing soccer.

glosses: used to show what happened after something else

examples.text: The alarm went off plus I woke up.

glosses: Something is invisible when we can not see it.

examples.text: Infrared light is invisible to animals and humans.
The magician made the woman invisible.

glosses: A jihad is a personal fight with yourself to become a better person.
A jihad is a holy war by Muslims to stop people from keeping down other people by force.

examples.text: The Muslims have started a jihad against the Israelis.

glosses: If you pay, you give money for something.

examples.text: Bess worked for eight hours and they paid her a hundred dollars.

glosses: Your pay is money you receive after doing something.

examples.text: Go to the office to receive your pay.

glosses: If you restore a state, feeling, or ability that has been lost, you make that possible or normal again.

examples.text: Police were sent to restore order after an attack on May 4.
The government attempted to restore confidence by announcing tougher laws.
With a simple operation, doctors were able to restore his hearing.

glosses: If you restore something, you make it go back to the way it was.

examples.text: The school is restoring the buildings that were damaged in the fire.
Art experts are working to restore the painting to its original condition.

glosses: If you restore something, you put or give it back.

examples.text: The lost child was restored to her parents by police.
Management has restored the extra vacation time.

glosses: An accumulation of something, is a number or amount of it that has come together over time.

examples.text: The failure to pump leads to an accumulation of blood in the heart.
There was an accumulation of dirt on the part of the floor people were walking on.

glosses: Accumulation is the process of bringing things together.

examples.text: The process of salt accumulation in the soil speeds up under poor watering conditions.
Private investment helped to boost capital accumulation.

glosses: An appendix is a part at the back of a book that has extra information.

examples.text: See Appendix B for a list of irregular verbs.
An appendix lists all 221 equations used by the program.

glosses: Your appendix is a small part of your body that is attached to your large intestine.

examples.text: It was common for children to die from a burst appendix.

glosses: If something is widespread, it happens or exists in many situations or places.

examples.text: This particular bird is only found here, but similar species are very widespread.
There is a widespread belief that when we are born we are like a blank sheet of paper.

glosses: If one thing accompanies something else, it comes or goes with it, or they happen together.

examples.text: She accompanied me to the hospital after my accident.
Children under 12 must be accompanied by an adult.
The text accompanying the illustrations is brief but helpful.

glosses: If person A accompanies person B on a musical instrument, B sings or plays the main part while A plays along.

examples.text: Joe Falcon sings and plays the accordion and is accompanied by Cleoma Breaux on guitar.

glosses: A prospect is what you think will happen in the future.

examples.text: There's a good prospect of this building being converted into a school.
Immigrants face the prospect of having to accept unskilled jobs at lower wages.
There is little or no prospect of a new station being opened up on the east coast.

glosses: Your prospects are your chances of moving forward in your job or in your life.

examples.text: So I would congratulate her on her good prospects as a teacher.
A new place offered some prospect of new beginnings.
We are very worried about her prospects.

glosses: A prospect is somebody that think will do well in the future.

examples.text: At 18, she is one of Britain's best prospects for an Olympic medal in Barcelona this summer.

glosses: A prospect is somebody who might be a customer or worker in the future.

examples.text: Your best prospects are your previous customers.

glosses: If you prospect for something valuable, such as gold or oil, you search an area for it.

examples.text: Anglo-United was not the only company prospecting for gold in the early eighties.

glosses: Post is the letters and parcels that you send to other people.

examples.text: There's no post today because it's a Sunday.
The new book arrived in the post.

glosses: A post is a tall rod or stick. Examples are a sign post, a lamp post, and a goal post.
If you post something, you send it through the post.

examples.text: I posted a birthday card to him last week.

glosses: If you post a message, you add it to a website or discussion board.

examples.text: I posted a reply to your comment on the website.

glosses: after

examples.text: Post the test results becoming public, there were many complaints.

glosses: A penny is a small coin of little value; 100 pennies (or 100 pence) make a pound, a dollar, a euro, etc.

examples.text: This sweet only costs a penny.
If you have two pennies, you have two pence.

glosses: If you hear a sound, you notice it with your ear.

examples.text: I heard music coming from the next room.
Speak louder, I cannot hear you!

glosses: A paragraph is one or more sentences that are written together with no line breaks separating them. Usually they are connected by a single idea.

examples.text: She knew what it would say after reading the first paragraph.
The crash was reported in a single paragraph in the Edinburgh Evening News.

glosses: If you paragraph something, you break it into paragraphs.

examples.text: It's hard to read with no breaks. Can you paragraph it out a bit?

glosses: Spic is an insulting word for a Latino or Hispanic person.
A petition is a written request to change something.
A petition is a list of signatures showing support for something or opposition against it.

examples.text: Please sign our petition to get a new snack machine in the school cafeteria.

glosses: A petition is a written document that people sign to show that they want a person or organization to do or change something.

examples.text: In honor of his memory, a petition has been sent to persuade the Postal Services Stamp Advisory Committee to put Willis Conover on a U.S. postage stamp.

glosses: To petition for something is to make a request for it, usually in writing.

examples.text: You should petition for a shorter work week.

glosses: A place's infrastructure is the basic public works such as roads, electricity & water supply, and schools, that allow it to function.

examples.text: The construction of the BAM railway will provide an infrastructure for exports to Japan and the US.
The new bridge will be one of Europe's largest ever infrastructure projects.

glosses: The infrastructure is the basic ideas and systems that support an organisation or a project.

examples.text: The hardware-software system provides an infrastructure for messaging applications across the company.

glosses: A deviation is difference or movement away from a standard.

examples.text: They insist that there must be no deviation from that style.
Any deviations from the contract would have to be agreed by both parties.

glosses: A deviation is the difference between a number and the average of a set of values.
A guideline is a formal suggestion about how something should be done, but it is not a rule.

examples.text: If you are a new driver you should try to follow these basic safety guidelines.
Our new guidelines will also say that we must be careful treat everyone equally.
The general guidelines for healthy eating stay the same.

glosses: A guideline is a line on a page that helps you see where to write or how to draw something.
A guideline is a rope or string that shows you where to go.
A commodity is something that is bought or sold.

examples.text: The price of corn and other farming commodities has dropped by 10%.
There have been big changes in commodity prices and exchange rates over the past decade.
Margaret had regarded her body as a tradeable commodity.

glosses: A commodity is a valuable quality or thing.

examples.text: Hope may become a very rare commodity.

glosses: If you minimise something, you make it as small as possible.

examples.text: We should take all steps to minimise the risk of disease.
We are trying to minimise pollution by using bikes instead of our car.
These steps will help us to minimise the time and cost of transporting materials.

glosses: If you minimize something, you make it as small as possible.

examples.text: We should take all steps to minimize the risk of disease.
We are trying to minimize pollution by using bikes instead of our car.
These steps will help us to minimize the time and cost of transporting materials.

glosses: Philanthropy is the giving away of money for charity.

examples.text: The man that lived in that mansion was admired for his philanthropy. He would often donate millions to charities.

glosses: A practitioner is a person who works in a profession or following a particular style or belief, especially related to health care.

examples.text: Acupuncture practitioners use fine needles to stimulate specific points of the body.
The book should be useful for new and experienced practitioners of yoga.

glosses: If something is challenging, it is not easy but it can be done.

examples.text: For a longer, wilder and more challenging route, you can explore the beautiful mountains around Goatfell.
All actors will agree that Hamlet is a very challenging role.

glosses: The present participle of challenge.
To name someone for a role or position, including that of an office.

examples.text: Jim nominated Tom to be the leader of their group

glosses: To name something for an award or prize.

examples.text: The movie was nominated for an Academy Award.

glosses: A radical change, difference, etc. is very big and important; from the roots.

examples.text: The plan will not be easy and requires a radical change in the culture of the city.
Many voices are calling for a more radical move away from the current situation.

glosses: A radial idea, policy, etc. is one that is new and different; not standard.

examples.text: More radical organisations like Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth have brought attention to these issues.
In a totalitarian society there is no more radical emotion than disbelief.

glosses: Of or about a root (e.g., √=2, the roots of plants, the root of a word, etc.)
cool

examples.text: Dude, that outfit is rad!

glosses: A radical is a person whose views are very different from most people.

examples.text: Leading radicals have called for a two-hour general strike on Monday.
These were young radicals, overturning the post war consensus, rolling back the state, liberalising markets, and transforming the political economy.

glosses: A quantity expressed as a root of another quantity. (e.g., √)
An atom or a group of atoms with at least one unpaired electron.
The basic part of a word to which other parts can be added (e.g., runner)
A radical is one part of a Chinese or Japanese written character that can be combined with other parts to form a whole character.
A chart is information that is organised in rows and columns or as a picture.

examples.text: In India as a whole the figure is about 40% (see chart).
This week's bar chart shows the correct figures.
You can write your weight in a diary or on a chart.

glosses: (often plural) A chart is a list of most popular songs, movies, etc. that is published regularly.

examples.text: This week, the newest Star Wars movie is topping the charts.

glosses: A map of seas or oceans.
If you chart something, you record it in a chart.
If something charts, it is on a list of most popular things.
If you "chart a course" you find out how to get somewhere.
A librarian is a person who manages a library.

examples.text: You can ask the librarian to help you find the book.

glosses: If you buy something, you give money and the thing becomes yours.

examples.text: Could you buy some milk at the store?
We sold the house and bought a small apartment near Lincoln Center.
I stood in line all night to buy tickets for the show.
My kids don't want to wear the clothes I buy for them.
I can't afford to buy a new house.
In 1960, Willard bought the business from his father.
He bought the guitar for $150 on the internet.

glosses: If money buys something, it is enough money to pay for it.

examples.text: $10 doesn't even buy a case of beer.
$100 buys a nice dinner or a hotel for the night.

glosses: If you buy (somebody) time, you stop something from happening soon so that you have time to prepare for it.

examples.text: She went to the washroom to buy time. She didn't want to answer before Kate arrived.

glosses: If you buy an idea, you believe it.

examples.text: Your mother won't buy the story about getting lost.
I can buy that your way works, but other ways might work too.

glosses: A buy is something that someone has bought, usually for a cheap price.

examples.text: This dress was a good buy. It was on sale.

glosses: If you are opinionated, you have opinions, especially strong opinions.

examples.text: She has strong feelings about many topics; she is an opinionated person.

glosses: The past tense and past participle of opinionate.
A word that sounds like another word, even though they have different meanings.

examples.text: "Right" and "write" are homophones.

glosses: A large organ in the body that makes bile, and controls chemicals in the blood.

examples.text: The liver is one of the most important organs in our body.

glosses: An organ used for food.

examples.text: We're having beef liver for dinner.

glosses: The colour of the liver, a dark brown.
The plural form of liver; more than one (kind of) liver.

examples.text: Livers produce bile.

glosses: An appreciation of something is the ability to see it's value and understand it.

examples.text: He now has a far greater appreciation of dogs and the people who handle them professionally.
The problems may have been due to a lack of appreciation of the different cultures.
Art appreciation can be learned, but it is very difficult to teach.

glosses: Appreciation is the feeling of being thankful.

examples.text: I just wanted to send you this card to show my appreciation for your kindness last week.
"You look lovely," he said, and she laughed with appreciation.

glosses: Appreciation is the rise in value of something.

examples.text: The appreciation of the Japanese yen against the US dollar has helped the American automobile industry.

glosses: A currency is the money from a particular country.

examples.text: A person going abroad can obtain foreign currency notes and travellers' cheques from his own bank.
The US dollar ended lower against most other currencies in London.
Since then the exchange value of the currency has fallen by 78%.

glosses: If something has currency, it is generally accepted.

examples.text: After the war, these new ideas began to gain currency.

glosses: The state of being up to date.

examples.text: A book's bibliography can be a good indicator of currency in the text.

glosses: Labor is the work that people do, usually lifting, moving, building, etc. rather than desk work.

examples.text: The cost of labor is higher than the cost of building materials.

glosses: Labor are the people who do this kind of work.

examples.text: There's a big labor shortage in the construction industry.

glosses: Labor is the process a pregnant woman goes through when she is giving birth.

examples.text: She was in labor for more than 12 hours before her baby was born.
Her labor was painful and slow. The doctors had to give her medicines to speed up her labor.

glosses: Labor is the name of a big political party in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand.

examples.text: Labor won the election.

glosses: If you labor, you work hard.

examples.text: He labored over the food all afternoon to get ready for dinner.

glosses: If you labor the point, you keep talking about it after people understand it well.
(also a sentence adverb) You use this to say that something cannot be avoided.

examples.text: A drop in the number of worker in a country inevitably leads to higher wages.
Inevitably, if you practice less, you will be less good.

glosses: A rumour is a story about somebody or something, that is told by other people, most of the time it is not true.

examples.text: There is a rumour going around that John's been fired. Is it true?

glosses: If you rumour, you gossip; you tell someone a rumor.

examples.text: It has been rumoured that John's moving soon. Is this true?

glosses: If you induce something, you make it happen.

examples.text: Soft lighting is often used for in restaurants to induce a feeling of relaxation.
He was given a drug which would normally induce sleep, but it had no effect on him.

glosses: A schedule is a plan of things that are happening and the times when they happen.

examples.text: He visits each village in his or her area on a weekly schedule.
The train is right on schedule.
The meeting was running 10 minutes ahead of schedule.
His doctors told him to cut down on his work schedule.

glosses: A schedule is a list, usually one with prices.

examples.text: Please see the enclosed schedule of costs for facilities and activities.

glosses: If you schedule something, you make a plan for when and where it will happen.

examples.text: The party was originally scheduled for June 5th.

glosses: Androgyny is hermaphroditism.
Androgyny is having both masculine and feminine characteristics.
Androgyny is looking neither masculine nor feminine.
The intensity of something is the amount of it in a given time or space.

examples.text: These flowers suffer from high intensity of sunlight.
It all depends on the intensity of the work, not the amount.

glosses: Intensity is a high level of power, strength, feeling, etc.

examples.text: Marie understood the intensity of the old woman's hatred.
The intensity of the pain made him scream.
She spoke with a new intensity.

glosses: You exhibit something when you show it to others.

examples.text: He exhibited the new product to the audience.

glosses: An exhibit is something that is shown to others.

examples.text: There is a new exhibit at the museum on the subject of Chinese history.

glosses: A bias is a preference in one direction that makes things unequal.

examples.text: There is strong evidence of a bias towards the death penalty for black rather than white murderers.
They had plans for an international centre, with a strong political bias.

glosses: The bias is the diagonal direction, especially in cloth.

examples.text: The neckline was cut on the bias to improve the drape of the fabric.

glosses: If you bias something, you unfairly make one result more likely than another.

examples.text: Sexism in language biases experience constantly towards the male sex.
By not providing this information, you bias the results.

glosses: Manipulation is the act of controlling someone or something, usually through pressure or in dishonest ways.

examples.text: The political manipulation of statistics to confuse people is common.
In data manipulation on a parallel computer all bits of a word are processed at the same time.
All too often, guilt is also a form of manipulation – a way of hurting or punishing others.

glosses: Manipulation is the act of using your hands skillfully to move, play or operate something.

examples.text: He tried to remove the piece by gentle manipulation from the outside.

glosses: A theme is a general idea that runs through a conversation, story, group of images, piece of music, etc.

examples.text: For Mr Giuliani, crime is a main campaign theme.
The topic did not seem related to the main themes of his studies.
The American novel focusses on themes of male companionship and confrontation with death.
They became a household name in 1982 with the theme music for the hit TV series, "Harry's Game".

glosses: If you theme something, you give it a theme.
The bulk of something is the largest part of it.

examples.text: The bulk of the shipment was headed for Toronto.
The great bulk of crime has always involved stealing of one kind or another.

glosses: Someone or something's bulk is its size or amount, especially if it is large.

examples.text: She took a deep breath, and, enormously grateful for the solid bulk of Leo at her back, she stepped inside.

glosses: If you sell something in bulk, it is not individually packaged.

examples.text: I usually buy nuts at the bulk food store.

glosses: If you buy something in bulk, you buy large amounts.

examples.text: The store offers discounts for buying in bulk.

glosses: A bulk is an item that is moved about like cargo.
If something bulks, it appears to be big in size.
If you bulk something, you increase its' size; you expand it.
If you do something on someone's behalf, you do it for them or as their representative.

examples.text: We give you this award on behalf of a grateful nation.
We have to leave, but would you please apologize to Steve on our behalf?
If you're not there, they'll make the decision on your behalf.

glosses: If you unify something or a group of things, you bring them together as one.

examples.text: When she explained it, all the different pieces of information and ideas came together for me in a unified whole.
There are many cultural, ethnic, historical, and geographical reasons why Ireland should be unified politically.
Music serves to identify and unify members of the group.

glosses: Erosion is the loss of land because of water and wind.

examples.text: Farming increases soil erosion by breaking up soil structure, and reducing the number of plants.
Footpath erosion is a significant problem in all the UK's national parks.

glosses: If you depress something, you push or hold it down.

examples.text: He depressed the button with his finger.

glosses: If something is depressed it is being made low.

examples.text: The prices were depressed by too much being available.

glosses: If something depresses you, it makes you very sad.

examples.text: Sad songs always depress me.

glosses: The comparative form of low; more low.

examples.text: New Orleans is lower than Denver.

glosses: If you lower something, you move it down.

examples.text: The man was lowered into the hole on a rope, so he could save the child.

glosses: If something is depressing it makes you sad.

examples.text: I find news about problems in the world depressing.

glosses: The present participle of depress. If you are depressing something, you are making it lower.
Someone or something that destroys.

If something (or someone) is destructive it destroys; it causes destruction.
Very strange or unusual. Very different from others of its kind or what is expected. Something that is weird is not at all normal.

examples.text: People laughed at the boy because he was weird.
Eating fish with chocolate syrup is so weird.
The strange man scared them because he looked weird.

glosses: If something destructs it destroys itself. Usually we say self-destruct instead.

examples.text: The weapon was made to self-destruct if stolen.

glosses: Self-destruct means to destroy oneself or itself.

examples.text: The weapon was made to self-destruct if stolen.

glosses: Algebra is a kind of mathematics where a letter (called a variable) can replace a number that is not known.

examples.text: Using algebra, we can define a line with the formula y=x+3

glosses: In some religions and myths, heaven is a place where you may go after you die. Heaven is usually seen as a happy place where good people are rewarded.

examples.text: I miss my grandmother, but I know she's with God in heaven.

glosses: The sky.
The skies or places in outer space.

examples.text: I looked up to the heavens in delight.
The planets make their way through the heavens.

glosses: Much happiness, or a cause of much happiness.

examples.text: He's been in heaven ever since we told him.
Our marriage has been pure heaven.

glosses: Alcohol is the chemical in some drinks that makes you drunk (intoxicated).

examples.text: Beer, wine, and whiskey all have alcohol in them.

examples.text: The scientist used an alcohol to fuel the burner.

glosses: The kind of mathematics in which addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division are done on numbers.

examples.text: My son is starting to do simple arithmetic like 2+2=4.

glosses: Magnification is the act or result of making something look bigger.

examples.text: The magnification of this small bug can help us see hidden details.
Things are easier to see at higher magnifications.

glosses: If you enjoy something, it gives you joy, happiness and pleasure.

examples.text: We enjoy dancing. When we dance, we feel happy and good.

glosses: A plant from South America.

examples.text: I love tapioca pudding, it's my favorite.

glosses: An expense is something for which you spend money.

examples.text: Food is a huge expense for many people around the world.

glosses: An expense is an amount of money that you spend.

examples.text: If your income is less than your expenses, you have a serious problem.
The company paid all of his expenses when he was in Shanghai.
The building was repaired at great expense.

glosses: If you do x at the expense of y, x hurts y because it makes y have less money, less time, less social status, etc.

examples.text: She often makes jokes at her own expense.
We have to decide whether safety at the expense of freedom is worth the cost.

glosses: Jazz is a kind of music invented by African Americans. It usually has a strong rhythm and is often played with horns.

examples.text: Duke Ellington and Glenn Miller were famous for playing jazz.

glosses: Nonsense.

examples.text: Stop talking jazz.

glosses: When two people marry they become husband and wife; that is, they become married. In many countries this is a legal agreement. In some cultures marrying is a part of the religion. Marrying is often done with a wedding (a special day for those people to marry).

examples.text: I cannot believe he married her when there are nicer girls out there.

glosses: If you marry two things, you connect them or make them into one thing.

examples.text: I have two different ideas I would like to marry together.
Music videos married music to television.

glosses: The life two people have together while they are married.

examples.text: The marriage seemed good until he left her.

glosses: When two people of becoming married; a wedding.
Two different things that have been made into one thing.

examples.text: Music videos are a marriage of music and television.

glosses: A wedding is a special time when two people marry each other.

examples.text: The wedding was very beautiful.

glosses: Two different things things that have been made into one thing.

examples.text: Music videos are a wedding of music and television.

glosses: The present participle of wed.
When people wed they become married. Wed is an old word, most people say marry now.

examples.text: I'd love to be wed, but I cannot find a girl to marry me.

glosses: When two things are wed they are made into one thing.

He is a non-believer; he does not believe at all.

glosses: Another word for you; thou is an old word, and people do not use it much anymore. Often when thou is used it is with other old words.

He accidentally put too much air in his flat tire. The air put so much pressure on the tire that it exploded.

His parents tried to pressure him into becoming a lawyer, but Jamal knew he wanted to be a doctor.

Ghosts are said to be souls of people who have died.

glosses: A ghost is the spirit or soul of a man.

This is my friend, Mary.

examples.text: Some people claim to have seen Mary appear to them.

glosses: If you are merry you feel happy.

glosses: If something is merry it makes people happy.

His family will be going back to merry old England soon.

I want to have a pretty painting in my house.

examples.text: The absent father was a comparative stranger to the son.

My students always forget the -er in comparatives.

glosses: Figures are numbers showing the value or amount of something.

examples.text: The sales figures from the spring were down from last year.
According to the official figures, unemployment levels are about 6 per cent.
You only have to look at the figures for fire deaths in hotels to see this is not a problem.

glosses: A figure is a person, often a well-known person.

examples.text: They have published articles about many leading figures including John Reed, J.A. Hobson, Tom Mann, and Daniel de Leon.
The figure of Margaret Thatcher towers over the Falklands War.

glosses: A figure is a person, especially the person's shape.

examples.text: She did not see the figure standing in the shadows of the kitchen doorway.
Across the river is the figure of Lenin on top of an armored car carved of stone.
Her girlish figure had disappeared as she aged, sat more, and ate more.
The most popular boy's toy ever is the G.I. Joe action figure.
He looked down at the wet figures of the boy and dog.

If x figures in something that happens, x is part of that happening.

examples.text: The weather figured prominently in their plans.
The fact that he wouldn't be there didn't figure among her worries.

glosses: If you figure that something is true, you think that it is true.

examples.text: Few people figured that he would win.

glosses: If you figure something out, you think about it until you understand it.

examples.text: He figured out that she was speaking Italian.

glosses: Sisterhood is the relationship between sisters.

When you speak of clothes in general, you speak of clothing.

examples.text: Shoes, shirts, and trousers are types of clothing.
You need to wear warm clothing in the winter.

glosses: The present participle of clothe.

examples.text: Clothing the poor is a goal for many societies.

glosses: A pattern is a design that uses the same set of elements many times in the same order.

examples.text: The table cloth had a simple pattern of red and white squares.

glosses: The combined qualities and activities for an individual or a group of people describes a pattern.

examples.text: The people of Spain have a pattern of resting in the afternoon and eating dinner late at night.

glosses: When you pattern something, you make it using a pattern.

examples.text: Much of crime fiction is patterned from true police stories.

glosses: When you provide something, you make it available.

examples.text: The restaurant provided food for the party.

glosses: Something is provided when an agreement or legal process requires it.

examples.text: Laws provide punishment for crimes.

glosses: When you provide, you give means of support.

examples.text: Parents try to provide for their children.

glosses: If something is pleasant, it is enjoyable or agreeable.

examples.text: When it rains in the summer, it is a pleasant event.

glosses: A pleasant person is one who is socially acceptable or polite.

examples.text: The man was pleasant with his smile and quiet laugh.

glosses: When we have speech, we have the ability to speak.

examples.text: Speech is a special human ability.

glosses: When we give a speech, we speak to a group of people.

examples.text: The valedictorian gave a speech to all of the students in his school.

glosses: If you fill something, you put something in it until there is no space left.

examples.text: She added some games to fill the gap in the schedule.
His eyes filled with tears as he watched her walk away.
She filled the car up with gas.
He's so mean, he just fills me with anger every time I think of him.
Suddenly, the screen was filled with light.
I fill up the dog's new dish to the top and stick it on the floor.
Instead of eating a good dinner she just fills up on bread.

glosses: If you fill in something, you give the missing information, especially personal information on a form.

examples.text: She gave me another form to fill in for housing benefit.
When I got back, she filled me in on what had been happening.

The full amount of food or drink that a person can eat or drink.

examples.text: Don't feed him any more, he's had his fill.
I've had my fill of alcohol for tonight.

glosses: Fill is extra material, often of low quality, used to give something more volume.

examples.text: They used the rocks as fill under the new house.

glosses: If you pass something, it was ahead of you and you move so that it is now behind you.

examples.text: Please, step to the right and let faster people pass on your left.
She was so close to the road that she could feel the wind from passing cars.
He looked in as he passed the window.
We passed through the tunnel and were back out into the light.
She passed her hand across her face.
He passed the belt through the loops in his pants.
Did you see two people pass this way, a man and a woman, walking north?

glosses: If a bill, law, motion, etc. passes, it is accepted, usually after a vote.

examples.text: The House passed a law that makes it a crime to have sex with anyone under age 16.

glosses: If you pass a test, exam, etc., you get a score that is good enough, often over 50%.

examples.text: You passed the test. In fact, you got 7 out of 10 correct.

glosses: If time passes, it moves from future to past.

examples.text: I'm bored here. The only thing that helps me pass the time is your letters.
They passed the night in a hotel just outside town.

glosses: If a road, river, railway, etc. passes a place, it continues from one side of the place to the other side.

examples.text: They are building a 150-kilometer road that passes through Yasuni Park.
The road from Karachi to Gadani passes the route once taken by Alexander the Great.

glosses: If you pass something to someone, you give it to them, usually by hand.

examples.text: Could you pass me the salt, please?
The book passed from hand to hand.
I passed your name on to my manager.
She passed the information on to the police.

glosses: If something passes, it happens.

examples.text: What has passed today must remain a secret.

examples.text: He passed to Lafleur, who put the ball in for the goal.

examples.text: We have a season's pass for the ski hill.

glosses: A pass is a score on a test, exam, etc. that is good enough, often over 50%. Also a person or paper that gets this score.

examples.text: On the last test there were only five passes; everyone else failed.
We have one of the highest pass rates for the exam in the state!

glosses: A pass is a throw, kick, hit, etc. of a ball, puck, etc. to another member of your team.

examples.text: Robert's pass in front of the net is blocked by the goalie.

glosses: A pass is a place in a mountain that is easy to travel.

examples.text: The mountain pass was blocked, which made it difficult to get across.

glosses: A pass is one case of a repeated action or process.

examples.text: We caught some new mistakes on the third pass.

glosses: A product is an item that can be bought.

examples.text: Skill is the product of hours of practice; His reaction was the product of hunger and fatigue.

glosses: A product is the number you get when you multiply two other numbers.

examples.text: The product of 2 and 3 is 6.

glosses: A product is a chemical substance that is made as a result of a chemical reaction.
When you prevent something, you stop it from happening.

examples.text: To prevent accidents, you must do everything with care.
No one can prevent us from going.

examples.text: The creation of a house takes time.

examples.text: The new dress was a great creation of beauty.

glosses: The time at beginning of the world and when God created everything is called creation.

examples.text: The Bible says that the creation took six days and God rested on the seventh.

glosses: The whole world is the creation in many religious traditions.

examples.text: The Bible says that God made all of the creation in six days.

glosses: If something is modern, it happened in current times.

examples.text: The new house has all modern conveniences.

glosses: Some new styles or forms of art and fiction writing are called modern.

examples.text: Much modern art looks odd to many people.

glosses: Extra; more than is needed.

examples.text: Usually it is not allowed, but in this particular case, it's OK.
I don't see any way to solve this particular problem.

glosses: A particular thing is a special or great one.

examples.text: She took no particular interest in what they were saying.

In particular, I'd like you to think about the first problem.

glosses: The particulars are the detailed information.

examples.text: The two stories are quite similar, though they differ in some particulars.
We've spent a good deal of time considering the particulars of the situation.

glosses: Finance is activities related to banking and money, especially by government.

examples.text: She had managed to raise sufficient finances to enable her and her family to travel to Australia.
The company's finances seem to be in good shape.

glosses: If you finance something, you provide money for it.

examples.text: The soccer team was partly financed by a local business.
The bank is financing our car loan.

glosses: If something finishes, it stops and doesn't start again; it comes to the end.

examples.text: I finish work at 4:30 and I get home at 5:00.
In June of 1992 I had just finished university and I was looking for a job.
She finished off her homework and put it away.
Finish up your lunch quickly, please.

glosses: If something finishes somebody off, it uses all their energy or it kills them.

examples.text: That last run around the track completely finished me off.

glosses: If you finish something up, you use the last of it.

examples.text: I finished up the milk this morning. There's none left.

glosses: If you are finished with something, you don't need it anymore.
If you finish the surface of something, especially wood, you make it smooth and ready to use.
The finish is the last part or end of something.

examples.text: As the runners come to the finish, they are side by side.
It was a good day from start to finish.

glosses: The finish is the way a surface looks after it has been made smooth and ready to use.

examples.text: The oil gives the wood a smooth, deep finish.

glosses: If you insure something, you pay money so that if something bad happens to it, you will get more money.

glosses: The past participle of wear.

glosses: If you invest your money, you use your money to make more money.

glosses: If you invest in something, you spend time or money to make it better.

examples.text: The province has invested $20 million to improve transportation in cities.
She invested all her spare time to make her small business succeed.

glosses: If you invest someone with a power, you give it to them.

glosses: A Japanese war cry.

glosses: A bateau is a light river boat with a flat bottom.

examples.text: The guide used a bateau to get us across the river.

glosses: A barrack is a building for soldiers to live and sleep in. The building is more commonly called barracks. A barrack used to mean "a temporary hut", but now is usually used for permanent buildings.

glosses: To shout or jeer at.

glosses: An assumption is a guess or belief about something without having enough information to know if it is true. In maths or science: something assumed to be true in order to build an argument or calculation.

glosses: A bible is any book that is considered an authority in a particular subject.

examples.text: The Blue Book is the bible for the value of used automobiles.

glosses: The Bible is name of the holy text of Christians consisting of a collection of writings of both Jews, called the Old Testament, and Christians, called the New Testament. (This is always spelled with capital B).
