glosses: The holy writings of the Jewish tradition, called the Old Testament, are called The Bible. (This is always spelled with capital B).

examples.text: The Jewish Bible has very old stories about the Jews.

glosses: A Bible or Bibles refer to copies of The Bible. This is always spelled with capital B).

examples.text: The book store sells many Bibles.

glosses: A book that is like the Bible but may be about another religion or is not religious. Often, this means a book that tells everything you need to know about something. Sometime this is used in a title to make a book sound very good.

glosses: If an activity involves something, then that thing is used in or is part of the activity.

glosses: A fever is when you are hot because you are sick and your temperature will be higher than normal.

glosses: AC is a short version of "alternating current" (a kind of electricity).

glosses: AC is a short version of "air conditioning" (cooling).

glosses: If something is likely, it is probably true or will probably happen.

glosses: You use likely to say that you think something is true or will happen.

glosses: A drum is a musical instrument with a skin that you hit to make music.

Sometimes I drum my fingers on my desk. (same meaning as above)

glosses: When something is acceptable it is capable of being accepted or is worth being accepted.

glosses: Drumming is the act of hitting a drum to make music.

When something is completely some quality, it is absolutely that quality, in every way.

examples.text: The man was completely honest in his business.
This is completely different from what people might believe.

glosses: When something is flexible, it can bend.

glosses: If you are successful, you are effective at something.

examples.text: The successful business man knows how to get money for his work.

glosses: If you have done something right, you are successful.

examples.text: The cook was successful when she made the best pepperoni pizza in town.

glosses: If you quit something, you stop doing it; that is, you do not do it any more.

glosses: If you quit a job, it means you are not going to work anymore. After you quit, you will no longer have that job.

If you have permission to do something, then the person who has authority over you or over that thing allows you to do it.

examples.text: My father gave me permission to go to the city.

glosses: If you give something a listen, you try to hear and understand it.

glosses: A load is something carried, often something heavy.

glosses: Load is the amount electrical power produced.

glosses: If you load a machine, you put in supplies that the machine uses.

examples.text: He loaded the gun, brought it up, and shot the deer in one continuous motion.

glosses: The Lord is a Judeo-Christian title for God.

examples.text: Please join me in the Lord's prayer.

glosses: A matter is something that you can talk about or do something about a topic or a situation.

examples.text: Government must make these changes as a matter of urgency.

examples.text: The students have all packed their bags and left for the summer.
It's time to pack up and go.

glosses: If you pack a place or a container with something (or pack something in a place or container), you put a lot inside.

examples.text: The hall was packed with visitors.

glosses: If you pack something like snow or earth, you press it to make it take up less space.

examples.text: All the runners had packed the earth hard.

glosses: If you pack a gun, you carry it with you.
If you pack something away, you put it away in a container.
If you pack it in, you give up.
A pack is a container that things are sold in.

examples.text: Cigarettes were selling for over $10 a pack.

glosses: A pack is a bag used to carry things, usually on your back.

examples.text: My spare clothes are in my pack.

glosses: A pack of cards is a set of 52 playing cards.
A pack is a group of animals, usually that hunt together.
A pack of people is a group, usually not a nice group.
A pack of lies is something that is completely untrue.
An ice pack is something cold that you put on an injury.
You use pardon to show that you didn't hear or understand someone.

examples.text: "Could you close the door, please?" "Pardon!" "Close the door, please."

glosses: You use pardon when you have made a rude sound like a burp.
If a government pardons somebody who is guilty of a crime, it allows them to live as though they had not committed the crime.

examples.text: The Ethiopian government has pardoned twenty five prisoners who were found guilty in connection to the unrest that rocked the nation.

glosses: When you pardon someone, you forgive them.

examples.text: I hope he'll pardon me for what I did to him.

glosses: You say pardon me or I beg your pardon when you didn't hear someone, when you accidentally touch someone, when you want someone's attention, or when you'd like someone to move.
A pardon is given when someone is forgiven.

examples.text: The soldier was given a pardon for all the acts he had committed while fighting in the war.

glosses: The plural form of penny; more than one (kind of) penny.

examples.text: These apples are twenty pence each.

glosses: A pension is money paid regularly by a government or company to someone who has stopped working, usually because of age or illness.

examples.text: When her pension ran out, she had to sell her house and move in with her daughter.
He regularly puts money into a retirement pension plan.
The employees do not like how the company is investing their retirement pension funds.

glosses: In Europe, a pension is a small hotel.

examples.text: I stayed at a pension during my trip to London.

glosses: A pension is what you pay for living in someone else's house or for staying at a small hotel.

examples.text: Did you remember to pay the landlady the pension?

glosses: If a company pensions a person, they force them to retire on a unpension.
When you pick something, you choose it.

examples.text: I have picked the best people to work on this job.
This was picked as the best new toy of the year.

glosses: If you pick up something, you lift it.

examples.text: She picked up the glass and put it down again.
Pick your clothes up off the floor!
The baby's crying. Can you pick him up?

glosses: If you pick up the phone, you answer it.
If you pick something up from somewhere, you go and get it.

examples.text: Mom, can you pick me up from Austin's at 8:00?
I'll go an pick up a pizza.

glosses: If you try to pick up someone you have just met, you talk to them because you want to have sex with them.
If you pick fruit, flowers, etc., you take them off the plant.

examples.text: We spent the morning picking apples in the forest.
Please help me pick up the books that I've dropped.

glosses: If you pick something from somewhere, you take it out of or away from that place.

examples.text: After dinner he picked the rice out of the children's hair.

glosses: If you pick a musical instrument such as a guitar, you play it by pulling its strings and letting them go.
If you pick at something, you touch it many times without doing anything.

examples.text: He was too sick to eat and just picked at his food.
She picked nervously at her dress.

glosses: If you pick on someone, you are not nice to them in particular.

examples.text: He was picked on by his brothers for his small size.

glosses: A pick is a choice.

examples.text: His pick for Man of the Year was John Smith.
You have your pick of the rooms. Which one do you want?

glosses: A pick is a tool used to dig.

examples.text: He dug that hole using a pick.

glosses: A pick is something used to play a guitar with.

examples.text: He forgot his guitar pick.

glosses: Actions or words that are politic are carefully chosen not to upset people.

examples.text: The senator gave a very politic reply.

glosses: political
The press are the people and organisations that report the news.

examples.text: The president gave an interview with members of the press.
The company put out a press release about the new equipment.

glosses: The press is the news as it is reported.

examples.text: The next day, the fire was all over the press.

glosses: A press is a company that prints books.

examples.text: The book was published by University of California Press.

glosses: A press is a machine that prints books, newspapers, etc.

examples.text: Stop the presses! We've got a new story.

glosses: A press is a machine that pushes down on something to make it flat or to push out the water or juice.
A press is a time when you push something.

examples.text: She gave the button a quick press.

glosses: If you press something, you push it against something.

examples.text: She pressed her nose against the window.
Please, press a button.
He found the cut and pressed down firmly to stop the blood.

glosses: If you press clothes, you use an iron to make them flat.
If you press someone to do something, you ask them strongly or many times.

examples.text: When she pressed him for an answer, he hung up the phone.
The group has been pressing for new laws to reduce pollution.

glosses: If you press on or forward, you keep going even though it's difficult.
If you press a weight, you exercise by moving the weight up and away from your body.
If you press a CD or record, you make a physical copy of it.
When you proceed, you go forward with something.

examples.text: The reporter proceeded with the interview.
They proceeded down the road.
After finding the money, he proceeded to put it in his pocket.

glosses: (formal) The proceeds of some individual project or sale are the money earned from doing it.

examples.text: We sold the house and bought a small apartment with the proceeds.
The proceeds of tonight's show will go to charity.

glosses: The proper way, place, use, etc. is the right one.

examples.text: What is the proper way to write a letter?

glosses: If something is proper, it is polite or acceptable.

examples.text: It's not proper for you to live alone like this.
She was a very proper young lady.
Why don't you get a proper job at a good company?

glosses: The x proper is the main or important part of x, not the parts near it.

examples.text: We stayed in a village and only went into the city proper during the day.

glosses: When you propose something, you say that it should be done or chosen, usually in a formal situation.

examples.text: She proposed that we should see a film.
We have proposed that a new group be set up to answer this question.
"I'm going to propose real cuts in taxes," said the President.
Clinton now proposes doing almost exactly the opposite.

glosses: When you propose a new theory or idea, you say that you believe it to be better than old ideas.

examples.text: I would like to propose that the problems we have had are actually not because of money.

glosses: When you propose to do something, you plan or intend to do it.

examples.text: What does he propose to do in the future?

glosses: If you propose to somebody, you ask them to marry you.

examples.text: He proposed to his girlfriend outside her house.

glosses: If you propose a toast, you celebrate somebody by raising a glass and drinking.

examples.text: I'd like to propose a toast to our new manager.

glosses: If something is rather large, different, difficult, etc., it is quite that way.

examples.text: I saw something rather unusual this morning.

glosses: When you would rather do something, you want to do it more than something else.

examples.text: I would rather see a film (than stay home).

glosses: instead of

examples.text: He went rather than stay behind and be alone.

glosses: You use or rather to change what you have just said.

examples.text: I went there, or rather I had planned to go there, last week.

glosses: You use rather to show that you agree strongly.

examples.text: "Did you like the movie?" "Rather!"

glosses: If you realize something, you become aware of it.

examples.text: John just realized that he had left his umbrella at home.
It took me some time to realize it was you.
Do you realize what you've done?

glosses: If something is realized, it is made real.

examples.text: My dreams of starting my own company have been realized.

glosses: When something is really a certain way, its very or very much that way.

examples.text: I really want to see a film.
I'm really hungry now.
You did a really good job on that.
Thank you for coming and helping me this morning. I really appreciate it.
I don't really like Japanese food.

glosses: If something really exists or really happens, it does exist or happen.

examples.text: Are you really going to the show?
Yes, I really will be there.

glosses: You can say "really?" when you are surprised.

examples.text: "He won yesterday." "Really?"

glosses: You can say "really" when you agree with something.

examples.text: "That girl talks about herself way too much." "Really. She's a nightmare."

glosses: Something that is recent has happened a short while ago.

examples.text: Has there been any recent news on the dispute?
In recent weeks, we have seen a big jump in the price of gas.
These changes are quite recent.

glosses: If you reckon that something is true, you think that it is true.

examples.text: What do you reckon we should do?
I reckon that he didn't know anything about it.
He's reckoned to be quite a good teacher.

glosses: If you reckon a number, cost, etc., you guess or calculate the value.

examples.text: I reckon the cost at about $23,000.
Reckoning from the map, Lexington to the headwaters of the Pedlar and back is forty-two miles.

glosses: If you reckon on something, you expect it.

examples.text: Oh dear, we didn't reckon on so many people.

glosses: If you reckon with somebody or something powerful or difficult person, you deal with them.

examples.text: In today's race, the Ethiopians will be a force to be reckoned with.

glosses: If you recognize something, you realize what it is.

examples.text: I don't recognize him. Is he a friend of yours?

glosses: If something is recognized, it is accepted.

examples.text: You have to recognize that you can't be right all the time.
The government refused to recognize his passport.
He's generally recognized as the person who made the first radio.

glosses: If something is recognized, it is given an award.

examples.text: John was recognized for his achievements as a scientist.

glosses: If something is reduced, it has been brought down or made smaller.

examples.text: The new computer system should reduce the number of problems.
This image is too large, could you please reduce the size?
Eating well will reduce the risk of heart disease.
Our time in the country was reduced to just a few days.
Taxes have been reduced by 24 percent.

glosses: If you reduce a liquid, you boil it to make it thicker.
If you refer to something, you talk or write about it, usually in passing.

examples.text: The teacher referred to some research, but I didn't know what he meant.
The media refers to the war as "the troubles".
He referred to her only by her first name.

glosses: If you refer to a book or other source of information, you check it.

examples.text: You should refer to the dictionary to find the meaning.

glosses: If x refers to y, x is about y.

examples.text: The numbers refer to last year's sales.

glosses: If you refer x to y, you send x to y for help or to be dealt with.

examples.text: He referred me to the science department.

glosses: If you have regard for something, you respect it.

examples.text: He has a high regard for his teacher.
These people have no regard for other people's feelings.

glosses: Regard is how something is though about or looked at.

examples.text: We do disagree, but only in regard to how much the government is spending.
What has he said with regard to taxes?
He's made a lot of money and is certainly a success in that regard.

glosses: You use Regards as a closing in a formal letter.
You ask somebody to give somebody else your regards as a formal way to show your concern for and interest in these people.
If you regard something, you think about it.

examples.text: How do you regard his actions?
She's widely regarded as the best tennis player in history.

glosses: When you regard something, you look at it.

examples.text: She regarded him with a smile.

glosses: If you remember something that you did or knew before, you can think of it again.

examples.text: He can't even remember where he left his books.
Writing my last story, I can't help but remember my first.
Sam was there, but I don't remember seeing anyone else.

glosses: When you remember something, you put it in your mind so you can think of it later.

examples.text: Please, try to remember how to spell the word.

glosses: If you remember to do something that you are supposed to do, you do it because you think about it.

examples.text: Please remember to ask before you take it.
Did you remember to get the milk?

glosses: A report is a description of something that has happened.

examples.text: There was a recent report on the election.

glosses: A report is a document that gives the results of a study of a particular situation.
A report is a loud fast noise.

examples.text: He could hear the report of the explosion.

glosses: If the news reports something, it tells us about it.

examples.text: The journalist reported that there were riots in the city.
He's been reporting on the ongoing war in Iraq.

glosses: When you report something that has happened, you describe it.

examples.text: They reported to the police that their car had been stolen.
She reported hearing loud noises at the time of the incident.
He's reported to have been there at the time.
So, you should report on your progress in three days.

glosses: If you report somebody for something they've done wrong, you tell an official about the problem.

examples.text: The restaurant was reported to the city because of the dangerous kitchen.

glosses: If you report somewhere, you go there and give your name.

examples.text: Visitors to the school should report to the office.

glosses: When you return something, you give/put it back.

examples.text: He returned the lawnmower back to John.

glosses: When you return to something or somewhere, you go/come back to it.

examples.text: He returned to China after his trip to Germany.
The main theme of the symphony's first movement returns in the last movement.
I've just returned from class, but I'll be leaving again soon.

glosses: If a feeling, problem, thought, etc. returns, it comes back.

examples.text: I thought I was better, but the pain in my back has returned.

glosses: If you return to an activity, you start it again.
If you return an act, you do the same act to the person who did it first.

examples.text: She turned her eyes towards him and he returned her her look.

glosses: If you return a ball in sports, you hit it back to the other player.

examples.text: He was unable to return serves all through the match.

glosses: If you return a profit or loss in business, you make it.
If you return something to a particular state, you make it that way again.

examples.text: We need to return the earth to a more healthy state.

glosses: Somebody's return is when they come back.

examples.text: They've planned a celebration for my return home.

glosses: Something's return is when it is given back.
A return is something that was bought but has to be taken back to the store, usually because it is broken.

examples.text: This store does not allow returns unless the customer has a receipt.

glosses: The return of something to a particular state is the change back to that state.
Someone's return to an activity is their restarting of the activity.
The return on money is the amount or percent of profit earned on it.
If you do something in return for something else, you do it to thank or pay back somebody; you make things balanced again.
The return of a feeling, problem, thought, etc. is when it comes back.
Return is a key on a computer keyboard that puts the cursor back at the beginning of a line.
A return is a form that you send to the government telling it about your income, your household, etc.
The returns in an election are the number of votes.
A return is a ticket that takes you where you want to go and back home again.
If you switch something, you change it to something else.

examples.text: He switched his book with mine.
We switched to a cheaper brand of coffee.
When they didn't seem to understand, he switched to French.
Jump ten times, switch legs and repeat.
I just switched jobs, and at my new job I don't have insurance.
When his team was losing, he switched sides.

glosses: If you switch a light or machine on, you change something so that it has power and can work.

examples.text: She sat up in bed and switched on the light.

glosses: If you switch a light or machine off, you change something so that it doesn't have power and can't work.

examples.text: I switched off the computer and went to bed.

glosses: If you switch over to something, you change to it, often with no plan to change back to the first thing.

examples.text: We used to watch CNN, but we've switched over to BBC World News.
It was difficult when I switched over from writing to acting.

glosses: If you switch gears, you change the way you think or act to match a particular situation.

examples.text: When I come home from work, it takes me a while to switch gears.

glosses: If you switch with somebody, you do something that they usually do and they do the thing that you usually do.

examples.text: Sibyl couldn't work on Tuesday, so I switched with her.

glosses: If you switch a machine to a particular setting or function, you set it to work that way.

examples.text: She switched the TV to another channel.
She switched the plane to automatic pilot.

glosses: A switch is what you use to turn lights or other machines and equipment on and off.

examples.text: The light switch is on the wall behind the door.
Where's the on/off switch on this printer?

glosses: A switch is a change from one thing to another.

examples.text: It's often difficult for older people to make the switch to living alone.

glosses: A switch is a place on the track where trains can chose between two tracks.
A switch is a networking device that connects networks together by sending data (packets) only to the devices that need them.

examples.text: Switches are more efficient than hubs because they understand which device needs the data that other devices send them.

glosses: A switch is a thin stick.
A term is a word or group of words, usually one with a special meaning in a particular field or area.

examples.text: They didn't know the meaning of the technical terms the doctor was using.
What is the definition of this term?
At age 10, she only knew that it was a term of abuse, a swear word.
She spoke in glowing terms about the progress they had made.

glosses: You use "in terms of" to introduce a topic or subject.

examples.text: Simply spending more money is not useful in terms of getting people back to work.
In terms of both numbers of people and size, California is one of the largest States in America.

glosses: If you talk about something in general/economic/human, etc. terms, you talk about it from that point of view.

examples.text: The changes are great in dollar terms, but the human cost is too high.

glosses: A term is a period of time.

examples.text: The President of Mexico is limited to serving a single term of six years.
He faces a maximum prison term of 15 years and $8.5 million in fines
The price may be up and down, but over the long term it will certainly rise.
The period of employment comes to term in three years.
She carried the baby to term.

glosses: A term is one of the times of year when school classes are held, usually September to December and January to April or June, also June to August.
A term is a number or symbol in a formula.

examples.text: The equation only worked when we included an extra constant term.

glosses: If you compare money or numbers in real terms, you compare the value on an equal basis.

examples.text: Today we are paying less for gasoline in real terms than we have at any time since 1918.
Although the absolute number of trucking accidents is up slightly, they are down 10 percent in the decade in real terms .

glosses: If you come to terms with something that is not nice, you accept it.

examples.text: He hasn't come to terms with the fact that she's not coming back.

glosses: The terms of a contract or purchase are its rules, conditions and limits.

examples.text: The company has announced generally agreement on a new contract though the exact terms still have to be worked out.
Under the terms of the purchase, we get the house on July 14th.

glosses: If two or more people or groups are on good/equal/bad etc. terms, they have a relationship that is good/equal/bad etc.
If two or more people or groups are on speaking terms, they are not close but do speak to each other.
If you term something a particular name or description, you give that name or description to it.

examples.text: The 1980s have been termed "The Forgotten Decade" by rock fans.
White House Spokesman Marlin Fitzwater termed the GNP growth "moderately healthy".
For lack of a better word, you might term it a police state.

glosses: When you suppose something, you guess that it is true.

examples.text: What do you suppose that he will do?
I suppose he'll come back. He always does.
I know I can't do it, but I suppose it's possible.
"You've been here about an hour, I suppose." "That's right."
Do you suppose that was his plan from the beginning?

glosses: You use I suppose to show that you agree weakly with something.

examples.text: "Did she know Paul pretty well?" "I suppose so."

glosses: You use I don't suppose to ask a question, especially when you think the answer is no.

examples.text: I don't suppose you remember me?

glosses: You use suppose to talk about an imaginary situation.

examples.text: Suppose, for example, that there was nothing there. Then what would you do?

glosses: A supply is an amount of something that you can use when you need it.

examples.text: We will need a supply of water.
During the war, the Americans destroyed their food supply.
Sadly these books are in very short supply in Britain.
The price of oil changes quickly to match supply and demand.

glosses: Supplies are things like food, water, medicine, gasoline, etc. that people need when they are not near somewhere where they can get them easily.

examples.text: The Japanese government is finally planning to send medical supplies and financial support.

glosses: Supply is the act or system of supplying something.

examples.text: They plan to fix the Russian economy and improve the supply of food and consumer goods.
The airplane's air supply wasn't working.

glosses: If you supply something, you make it available, usually regularly.

examples.text: We were supplied with a few basic tools that we needed for the job.
Our garden supplies us with all the food we need.
The office was well supplied with chairs.

glosses: In a supple way.
If something succeeds, it has happened the way somebody wants it to happen.

examples.text: He succeeded in getting everyone to like him.

glosses: If you succeed, people recognize that you are good at what you do.

examples.text: It's more difficult for women to succeed in business.

glosses: If x succeeds y, x replaces y.

examples.text: The new king succeeded his father.
DVDs succeeded VHS as the main way to watch movies.

glosses: Something that happens soon happens shortly after another time, often shortly after the time of speaking.

examples.text: Why did he call me so soon? Did something bad happen?
John is coming home soon.
How soon will it be ready?

glosses: If x happens as soon as y does, x happens right after y.

examples.text: As soon as he finished eating, he got up and walked away from the table.

glosses: If something is soon, it is shortly after another time, often shortly after the time of speaking.

examples.text: He wanted to leave, but it seemed too soon.
There will be a time when we'll need a new school, and that time will probably be soon.

glosses: A slight increase, difference, etc. is a small change.

examples.text: This year's 5.6% level is a slight increase from last year's 5.4%.
Don't worry about me. It's just a slight pain
I don't have the slightest idea what she meant.

glosses: If someone is slight, they are thin.

examples.text: Out stepped a slight, middle-aged woman who smiled kindly.

glosses: If you slight someone, you treat them as if they were not important.

examples.text: Ever since that time, he's been slighted by his fellow workers.

glosses: A slight is when you are not polite to someone.

examples.text: Has she forgiven him for his slight?

glosses: If something is situated somewhere, it is there.

examples.text: The school is situated in a mostly-white area.

glosses: You use sir to speak or write to a man formally to be polite.

examples.text: Excuse me, sir, could you tell me where the nearest bookstore is?

glosses: Sir is a title used before certain men's names.
A single thing is the only one.

examples.text: In large baking dish, arrange chicken pieces in single layer.

glosses: You use single to stress how many or how few.

examples.text: I hate going to work every single day and listening to people yell at each other.
I haven't heard a single word of thanks.
Eastern Canada is the world's largest single source of newsprint.
I don't think we should give them a single thing.

glosses: A single person is not married.

examples.text: The single mother of two spends weekends with her kids.
I used to go out a lot when I was single.

glosses: A single is a song that is sold or put out by itself (or with one other song), not on an album.

examples.text: Today she releases her live version of Birthday, the first single from an upcoming tour album.

glosses: In baseball and cricket, a single is a hit that enables a runner to score a point.
In baseball a single is a hit that enables the player to move to first base.
Singles is a game where each side has only one player, especially in tennis.
Singles are people who are not married or not in a romantic relationship.

examples.text: You'll pay no tax if your income falls below $50,000 for a married couple, $35,000 for singles.

glosses: A single is a hotel room for one person.

examples.text: I reserved a single in Montreal.

glosses: In baseball if you single, you hit the ball and are able to run to first base.

examples.text: The batter singled to right field.

glosses: If you single something out, you identify it, often to give it special attention.

examples.text: She was singled out as the best student in the class.

glosses: A sheet is a flat cloth that you cover a bed with.

examples.text: Use the sheets next to the bed.
He wanted to sleep between clean white sheets in his own bed.

glosses: A sheet is a single piece of paper.

examples.text: Can I have a sheet of paper?

glosses: A sheet is a thin flat thing, usually something square or rectangular.

examples.text: Place the rolls on the baking sheet.
A sheet of ice covered the ground.

glosses: A line (rope) used to adjust the trim of a sail.
If you settle a fight, argument, case, etc., you find an answer that stops it.

examples.text: They settled the dispute. Both men were happy with the results.

glosses: If something is settled, it is decided.

examples.text: OK, it's settled: we're going to Florida this summer.

glosses: If something settles, it moves to a position where it can stay in for a long time, often in a low position.

examples.text: She got a drink and then calmly settled herself in front of the TV.
After the crash, it took some time for the dust to settle.
His eyes settled on the red flower.
The put the earth back into the hole. It was high, but it would settle in time.
A feeling of sadness settled over them.

glosses: If you settle for something, you accept it even though it is not as good as you wanted.

examples.text: This year, she would have to settle for third place.

glosses: If you settle a place, you move there and live there.

examples.text: After moving to Canada, they settled in Toronto.

glosses: If something settles (down), it becomes still and quiet.

examples.text: The noisy class needs to settle down.

glosses: If you settle (up) a bill, or your affairs, you pay the money you owe and/or receive the money that others owe you.
If your stomach settles, it doesn't feel sick anymore.
When you serve food or drink, you give it to somebody to eat or drink, especially as a host.

examples.text: Shall I serve your drinks first?
Lunch is served from 11:00 until 3:00.

glosses: If something serves (as something), it used or useful for a certain purpose.

examples.text: This cup can serve as a holder for my paintbrushes.
This program has served as a model for smaller enterprises throughout the state.
His experiences during the war served as the basis for his book.
The area is served by a number of schools.
The law no longer serves the function it once did.

glosses: When you serve (as something), you work.

examples.text: John served in the army.
He served as the director of the company from 1992 until 2003.
He serves the king.

glosses: If you serve time in prison, you stay there because you are a criminal.
If you serve, in a game like tennis, you begin play by sending something like a ball over a net.
A serve in a game like tennis is the action beginning of play by sending something like a ball over a net.

examples.text: Whose serve is it?
That was a great serve!

glosses: A sale is the act of selling something.

examples.text: Proceeds from the sale of the art went to the local school.
The sale of guns in Canada is tightly controlled.

If a sound in a word is rhotic, it has the sound the letter r makes in most American, Canadian, and Irish ways of talking.

If a dialect (form of a language) or accent is rhotic, it uses this sound after a vowel: often used in dividing English accents into the rhotic and the non-rhotic. (Note that all accents of English pronounce the rhotic sound if "r" or "rh" is immediately followed by a vowel – which means it is always pronounced at the start of a word.)

If a dialect (form of a language) or accent is non-rhotic, it only pronounces the rhotic sound for the letter R when it is before a vowel (more precisely, the rhotic sound is pronounced if "r" or "rh" is immediately followed by a vowel – which also means it is always pronounced at the start of a word). Most British accents in England and Wales are non-rhotic (with the notable exception of West-Country accents), as are all Australian accents and most accents of Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Maine in New England, United States.

Buridan's ass is a philosophical question that can be summarized like this: A hungry ass (donkey) is placed in between two bales of hay. The donkey needs to eat at least one of the bales of hay, otherwise it will starve and die. Assuming that free will does not exist and that the donkey decides purely based on logic, how does the donkey decide which hay bale to eat?
